items.title: Elvin Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Let’s see: McCoy, then McCoy’s brother in law Steve Davis, and that was it.

ctx.x: Who else was in that band?
Let’s see: McCoy, then McCoy’s brother in law Steve Davis, and that was it.
Yes, it was a quartet. So Billy Higgins played the first set, did you play that same night?

items.title: Tyner McCoy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: a lot of your projects you bring EJ, Elvin Jones back in, there’s that sympatico, that very close relationship you have with him

ctx.x: I like the sound of it. It was considered the Japanese piano before they started making pianos themselves. I enjoyed it, and I heard a lot of it when I was in Japan, so it was fascinating. Fooling around with it, I would pluck it. I didn’t study the instrument so I couldn’t say I was going to play it. I use it on some recordings on the intro. Anyway, it was very fruitful experimenting with different things.

So I look at your long tenure, a lot of your projects you bring EJ, Elvin Jones back in, there’s that sympatico, that very close relationship you have with him. When I think of Sahara, now you have Alphonse Mouzon.

Yeah (laughs) he was quite a character, he was a good guy. He was a character in a lot of ways, I liked him, he was eccentric, but it was good, he didn’t mind trying things. You know, he’d say, “I got an idea,” he would jump in there and do it, you know, he was very musical in his own way. There were times maybe, I didn’t restrict him but, “Chill here a little bit, we’ll work on it and get it.” He was willing to work with you, he wasn’t the kind of guy that was like, “Well my way is the best way,” he wouldn’t do…
